questions.problem:
Find the velocity of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$

$v(\frac{\pi }{4})\,=\,$
{{field-1}}$\text{m/s}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14259041/assets/dbf36192ac332dc49ed75278838e989a37ac7d888311be1b8b059a7b59667aa6.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{\pi }{4}$ corresponds to the point $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}).$

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})}=\frac{1}{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}=\sqrt{2}.
$$

Finally, evaluating $v(t)$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ we have

$$
3{csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=3{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}=6.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Substituting $t=0$ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to {0}^{+}}v(t) & ={lim}_{t\to {0}^{+}}3{csc}^{2}⁡t \\  & =3{csc}^{2}⁡(0) \\  & =3\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡(0)} \\  & =\frac{3}{{(0)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{0},\end{aligned}
$$

which is undefined.

Therefore, to find the limit, let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{csc}⁡t.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14259041/assets/b01f56f0a78beb3b13799265975b1f4b16614e4a77d08aa24e024cf88309c4fc.png)

As $t$ approaches $0$ from the right, the values of $y=\operatorname{csc}⁡t$ are positive and grow without bound. 

Therefore

$$
{lim}_{t\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{csc}⁡t=\infty 
$$

Applying the product and power rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to {0}^{+}}3{csc}^{2}⁡(\pi ) & ={lim}_{t\to {0}^{+}}3\cdot {lim}_{t\to {0}^{+}}{csc}^{2}⁡(t) \\  & =3\cdot {({lim}_{t\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{csc}⁡(t))}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying by the positive constant $3$ does not change the sign of the limit, so we have

$$
3\cdot {({lim}_{t\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{csc}⁡(t))}^{2}=\infty .
$$

questions.problem:
The acceleration $a(t)$ of the particle is given by the derivative of the velocity with respect to time. Find the function $a(t).$

$a(t)=$
{{field-1}}$\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡t$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write

$$
v(t)=3{csc}^{2}⁡(t).
$$

Now, we see that $v(t)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
v=3{u}^{2},\,u=\operatorname{csc}⁡t.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}u}=6u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=-\operatorname{csc}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & ={v}^{′}(t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t} \\  & =6u\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t) \\  & =(6\operatorname{csc}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t) \\  & =-6{csc}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Another particle has a velocity function given by ${v}_{2}(t)=t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).$ Evaluate the velocity of this particle at $t=\frac{5\pi }{3}.$

${v}_{2}(\frac{5\pi }{3})\,=\,$
{{field-1}}$\text{m/s}$
questions.worked_solution:
Evaluating the function ${v}_{2}(t)$ at $t=\frac{5\pi }{3}$, we get

$$
{v}_{2}(\frac{5\pi }{3})=(\frac{5\pi }{3})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{20\pi }{3})
$$

First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $\frac{20\pi }{3}$ that lies in the range $[0,2\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{20\pi }{3}-6\pi  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{20\pi }{3})=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}).$

Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14259041/assets/dbf36192ac332dc49ed75278838e989a37ac7d888311be1b8b059a7b59667aa6.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{2\pi }{3}$ corresponds to the point $(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}).$

Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})=-\frac{1}{2}.$

Therefore, $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{20\pi }{3})=-\frac{1}{2}.$

Finally, 

$$
{v}_{2}(\frac{5\pi }{3})=(\frac{5\pi }{3})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{20\pi }{3})=-\frac{5\pi }{6}.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
In part 3, we saw that the derivative of a particle's velocity with respect to time gives its acceleration.

To differentiate ${v}_{2}(t),$ we require the product rule. Let $g(t)=t$ and $h(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).$ Then

$$
{g}^{′}(t)=1,\,{h}^{′}(t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

We used the chain rule to calculate ${h}^{′}(t).$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2}(t) & ={v}_{2}^{′}(t) \\  & ={g}^{′}(t)\cdot h(t)+g(t)\cdot {h}^{′}(t) \\  & =(1)(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))+(t)(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).\end{aligned}
$$
